prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into the theory of international trade, and thereby transforming how the gains from trade and the choice between exporting and foreign investment are understood

statement.case_for: Firm heterogeneity with selection into exporting (Melitz 2003; Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple 2004) is a conceptual change in how a whole field models and measures its central question. It moved trade analysis from representative firms and industries to reallocation across heterogeneous firms. That opened a new channel for the gains from trade and a firm-level empirical agenda that is now routine in policy evaluation. It also carries into macro and growth work on productivity and reallocation, and into quantitative general-equilibrium modelling, which is the tradition I know best. More than twenty years of replication, structural extension and use mean maturity is not a concern. The core credit also traces to a short list of papers: Melitz for the selection model, and Helpman, with Melitz and Yeaple, for the exports-versus-FDI sorting result, building on Helpman's earlier monopolistic-competition trade theory. In my opening I ranked B006 first and B001 second. After reading colleagues' attribution arguments I moved B001 to the top, mainly because its attribution is cleaner and its discovery boundary is tighter. I am not relying on how many colleagues ranked it first, since that is not evidence of scientific merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made closely related contributions, including the empirical facts on exporter premia and the Ricardian-heterogeneity lineage, and none of them is credited on this ballot entry. A two-name prize therefore risks looking narrow, and Redding's quantitative and spatial work is excluded. Part of the broader new-trade-theory lineage was also recognised in 2008, and some detailed predictions of the baseline Melitz model are rejected in data, with welfare implications that depend on distributional assumptions. B001 is also a theory-led contribution with a more indirect link to policy than B006's direct use in antitrust and merger practice.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B006 first. He argues that BLP demand estimation and Pakes's dynamic industry models changed empirical industrial organisation, are standard in antitrust and merger analysis, and tie data to theory. He also notes that industrial organisation has not been recognised since 2014, and that three names capture the central idea cleanly.
responses.response: I ranked B006 first myself and still think its impact is very large and fully mature. Strömberg's own uncertainty has made me weigh the boundary problem more heavily. It is unclear whether BLP demand estimation and the Pakes dynamic-games strand are one discovery or two, and Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are all arguable. I would not treat the time since the last IO prize as a merit argument. B001 has a sharper discovery boundary and a more settled credit story, so I now place B006 as my first alternative. If the Committee judges that B001's attribution gap is too large, B006 remains an entirely credible fallback for me.

responses.point: Andersson proposes Helpman and Melitz and leaves out Redding. In his view Redding's quantitative and spatial work is a later extension and less central to this specific discovery. He also raises whether Helpman might be better paired with someone else for a different trade citation.
responses.response: I agree on leaving out Redding. His quantitative and spatial contributions build on the selection framework rather than originate it, and I judge the priority question separately from influence. I would not bring a different Helpman pairing into this round, because it is outside the shortlisted ballot IDs. On B001 the case rests on the heterogeneous-firm selection and sorting results, which is why my citation names those and not Helpman's wider trade theory.

responses.point: Boppart notes that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are parallel contributors outside the credited set, which limits a clean two-person attribution. He adds that Krugman's earlier prize covered part of the new-trade-theory lineage.
responses.response: This is the most serious qualification to B001, and I take it seriously. It is why I keep the citation tied to the theoretical selection mechanism and the export-versus-FDI sorting result, which are the contributions of Melitz and of Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple, and why it does not claim the whole firm-level trade literature. Empirical precursors and the Ricardian-heterogeneity line can be acknowledged in the scientific background without being credited, since the Committee can only cite the names on the ballot. On Krugman, 2008 recognised love-of-variety, scale and location in new trade theory. Selection and reallocation across heterogeneous firms is a distinct conceptual step with its own channel for the gains from trade, so I do not see duplication.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee views the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not credited on this ballot entry, as a disqualifying attribution gap or as acknowledgeable in the background.
Whether B001 and B006 can be combined: the five credited people exceed the three-person limit, and a trimmed pairing such as Pakes alone would fragment the BLP credit.
Whether B006's boundary between demand estimation and dynamic industry models, and the roles of Bresnahan and Reiss, are resolvable enough to keep it as a serious alternative.
I have not independently verified citation counts or priority records; this assessment rests on the supplied evidence and general knowledge.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for B001, B006 or B034. My profile ties are co-authorships and colleague relationships with Krusell, Boppart and Friberg, none of whom is a credited name on these ballot entries, and my own research is not among the shortlisted discoveries.
